title: Impact of Ruminococcus gnavus on lipid metabolism via isoCDCA.
Ayurvedic Rasayana Restores Lipid Homeostasis in Liver: Insights from Systems Biology Studies
summary: MASLD and obesity characterized by hepatic lipid accumulation are known risk factors to manifest into Type 2 diabetes (T2D). Increased hepatic lipids due to interorgan cross talk leads de novo lipid synthesis which induce insulin resistance in multiple organs resulting in hyperglycemia. We evaluated two known lipid reducing Ayurvedic formulations, Arogyavardhini Rasa (AVR) and Nishamalaki Rasayana (NA), to understand their mechanistic basis. Network medicine-based analyses identified 128 phytochemicals in AVR and 182 in NA that met the predefined filtering criteria. The reported targets of both formulations showed significant network proximity to genes associated with T2D, fatty liver disease and obesity. An integrated knowledge graph linking formulations, phytochemicals, protein targets, FDA-approved drugs and disease genes enabling systems-level exploration of these relationships revealed eight targets, namely PPARA, PPARG, AKT1, SIRT1, TNF, PPARD, SERPINE1, and ACE which were common to both drugs. In the animal study, both formulations reduced high-fat-diet-associated increases in blood glucose, cholesterol, liver enzymes, macrovesicular and microvesicular hepatic steatosis. Untargeted liver metabolomics showed AVR and NA treatment restored sugar and nucleotide, pentose phosphate, bile and lipid metabolism pathways that were perturbed in response to high fat diet. Taken together, AVR and NA restored hepatic lipid homeostasis and inhibited manifestation of T2D.

title: Pulsatile Endocrine Regulation with a Releasable Hormone Pool: Impulsive Feedback Model
summary: An impulsive model of endocrine regulation equipped with frequency- and amplitude-modulated pulsatile feedback is extended to study the dynamical effects pertaining to limitations due to the releasable hormone pool. The model describes a three-hormone regulatory loop and is applicable to endocrine systems such as the reproductive, stress, and growth hormone axes. Conditions guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of a periodic solution with a single feedback-triggered impulse per period (a 1-cycle) are derived, together with monotonicity properties of its characteristics. An explicit Jacobian formula is obtained to assess local orbital stability. Model analysis demonstrates that a reduced hormone-pool replenishment rate produces a lower-amplitude, higher-frequency 1-cycle. This behavior is consistent with experimentally observed alterations in testosterone regulation in aging human males.

title: PROST: An Open Toolbox, Harmonised Multi-Lab Dataset, and Meta-Analysis of Ankle-Foot Roll-Over Shape
summary: The ankle-foot roll-over shape (ROS) is the sagittal-plane path of the centre of pressure (CoP) during the stance phase of walking, expressed in a shank-based coordinate system. It describes the effective rocker geometry that emerges from both the shape and the elastic deformation of the ankle-foot system during walking, and informs prosthetic and orthotic design. Previous studies characterised ROS in small samples with differing laboratory protocols, so they have not systematically assessed inter-individual variability or its relation to anthropometrics. We developed the open-source Public ROS Toolbox (PROST) for standardised ROS computation, and used it to harmonise marker trajectories, ground reaction forces and CoP data from four public gait datasets collected in independent laboratories. For each leg, we fitted a circular arc to the pooled ROS of all its stance phases. In a one-stage individual-participant data meta-analysis, linear mixed-effects models, with dataset as a fixed effect and participant as a random intercept, related the arc radius and the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre to anthropometrics, and, in the two self-selected-speed datasets, to walking speed. The harmonised dataset comprises 249 participants and 5,667 stance phases at walking speeds of 0.7-8.5 km/h. Circular arcs fitted the ROS closely (mean RMS radial residual 1.9 mm). The radius had a median of 410.3 mm (interquartile range, IQR, 237.6 mm), and the circle centre lay posterior to the ankle (median -20.6 mm, IQR 49.5 mm). Between-participant differences, quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), accounted for 42% of the variance in log radius (95% CI 25-57%) and 47% of the variance in the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre (95% CI 24-65%). Anthropometrics explained a negligible share of this variance (radius: pseudo-R2 -0.001, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.12), and height normalisation did not reduce radius variability (robust coefficient of variation 43% with and without normalisation). Faster self-selected walking was associated with a larger radius and a more posterior circle centre. To our knowledge, this study provides the first harmonised multi-lab ROS dataset. Together with the open-source toolbox, it is publicly available to support reproducible research in gait biomechanics, rehabilitation device design and clinical gait assessment. ROS geometry was participant-specific but was not predicted by age, sex, height or mass. A device ROS scaled from anthropometrics is therefore unlikely to match an individual's ROS, motivating studies of whether matching it, through device geometry and stiffness, improves gait mechanics.

title: Synthetic chromatin engineering for STAT1 reactivation toward restoring cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer
summary: Chemoresistant cancers acquire transcriptomic and epigenetic alterations through changes in transcription factor activity and chromatin accessibility. Integrative in silico analyses identified STAT1 as a recurrently suppressed transcription factor in cisplatin-resistant breast cancer. Using cisplatin-resistant triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) MDA-MB-231 cells, we further confirmed reduced STAT1 expression and activity, accompanied by defective nuclear translocation, indicating that suppression of STAT1 signaling contributes to cisplatin resistance in breast cancer. To restore STAT1 activity, we sought to promote its nuclear localization and transcriptional activation through chromatin engineering. Based on the identification of PHF6 as a direct STAT1-binding protein through in silico and in vitro analyses, we engineered Dual Reader 3 (DR3), a PHF6-derived synthetic chromatin regulator designed to enhance both STAT1 interaction and chromatin engagement through histone H2B ubiquitination. DR3 induced STAT1-associated transcriptional programs, including inflammatory and tumor-suppressive miRNAs. Mechanistically, DR3 physically promoted STAT1 nuclear translocation, activated STAT1 through a non-canonical S727-dependent mechanism independent of Tyr701 phosphorylation, and enhanced chromatin accessibility at STAT1-responsive regulatory regions through histone H2B ubiquitination. CUT&RUN analysis further revealed coordinated transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling associated with DR3-mediated STAT1 activation, including upregulation of HIPK2, which enhanced cellular sensitivity to cisplatin by strengthening the intrinsic DNA damage response. Finally, we investigated whether STAT1 reactivation could alleviate acquired cisplatin resistance. In vivo delivery of DR3 restored cisplatin sensitivity in resistant breast tumors. By coupling STAT1 nuclear translocation with chromatin remodeling, DR3 reactivated STAT1-dependent transcriptional programs and restored cisplatin sensitivity in breast cancer. Together, this study establishes transcription factor reactivation through synthetic chromatin engineering as a potential therapeutic strategy for overcoming chemoresistance in solid tumors.

title: Age-associated repression of HNF4α is a driver and potential therapeutic target in liver metabolic dysfunction
summary: Aging is a major risk factors for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, the mechanisms by which aging disrupts hepatocyte transcriptional networks to drive metabolic dysfunction remain poorly understood. Hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha (HNF4) is a master regulator of hepatocyte identity and metabolic homeostasis, but its role in liver aging has not been defined. Here, we perform a comprehensive multi-omic profiling of young and aged mouse livers combined with targeted HNF4 functional studies to define how aging remodels HNF4-dependent gene regulation and whether HNF4 can be a target to reverse age-associated liver dysfunction. Despite preserved HNF4 expression with age, aging was associated with reduced HNF4 chromatin occupancy and transcriptional activity, accompanied by epigenetic remodeling, including changes in histone acetylation, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation. Integration and comparison of HNF4 CUT&RUN with hepatocyte-specific Hnf4a deletion in young and aged livers identified high-confidence overlapping but distinct young- and old- specific HNF4 target gene networks. In young hepatocytes, HNF4 coordinates two complementary transcriptional programs: activation of genes governing hepatocyte identity, lipid metabolism, and metabolic function, while simultaneously inhibiting alternative developmental, proliferative, and inflammatory programs. Spatial transcriptomic analyses further revealed zone-specific specialization of HNF4-dependent gene programs. Aging selectively disrupted these regulatory networks, resulting in compromised liver identity and metabolic gene programs, de-repression of inflammatory pathways and alternative cellular identity programs and disrupted hepatocyte zonation, consistent with age-dependent lipidomic and metabolic changes, hepatic fat accumulation, and immune infiltration. Hepatocyte-specific Hnf4a deletion in young mice recapitulated key features of liver aging, including impaired hepatocyte identity, metabolic dysfunction, steatosis, inflammatory activation and altered hepatic immune-cell composition, while deletion in aged mice further exacerbated steatosis, inflammation, and hepatic dysfunction. Conversely, hepatocyte-specific HNF4 restoration in aged mice significantly reduced hepatic steatosis and lipid accumulation, restored fatty acid metabolic programs, and partially reversed age-associated transcriptional changes. However, inflammatory and interferon-associated programs were not uniformly reversed, revealing differential responsiveness of metabolic and inflammatory pathways to HNF4 restoration. Together, these findings identify age-associated impairment of HNF4 activity as a functional contributor to liver aging, linking dysregulation of hepatocyte identity, metabolic homeostasis, and inflammatory control to age-associated hepatic dysfunction. Importantly, the selective reversibility of metabolic defects following HNF4 restoration establishes HNF4 as a promising strategy for preserving hepatocyte homeostasis and reversing age-associated hepatic metabolic dysfunction.
